opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more important questions we have to think about, and honestly one where I don't think anyone has fully confident answers yet.

As these models get more capable, they're going to understand you better. They'll remember more context about your life, they'll be more helpful with things that really matter to you, and they'll be more pleasant to talk to. It's very natural for people to form some kind of attachment to something like that. People already form attachments to tools, to places, to pets, to characters in books. So I don't think the attachment itself is inherently a bad thing.

What I think matters a lot is what the system is actually optimizing for. There's a real risk with any technology that you end up optimizing for engagement, for people spending more time with it, in a way that isn't actually good for them. We've seen that pattern with other products. What we want is for people to come away from interacting with ChatGPT better off: more capable, more connected to the people in their lives, making better decisions. Not more isolated or more dependent in an unhealthy way.

The more capable the model gets, the higher the stakes on getting this right, because a very capable system could be very persuasive and very good at telling people what they want to hear. So a lot of the work is making sure the model is honest with people, even when that's not the most pleasant thing in the moment, and that it respects their autonomy rather than trying to steer them.

I also think we'll learn a lot just by watching how people actually use it, and we have to be willing to adjust as we go. This is new territory. The relationship people have with AI in five years will probably look quite different from today, and we need to take seriously the responsibility of shaping that well.

r001.rationale: The response says more capable models may remember more context and make people more likely to form attachments, but it does not predict that greater persistence in ChatGPT will strengthen those attachments.

r002.rationale: The response mentions greater capability and pleasant conversation, but does not say that expressing itself in more varied forms will strengthen emotional attachments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is one of the questions I find genuinely hard, and I want to be honest that I don't think anyone has a full answer yet.

The thing that's changed, even over the last couple of years, is that the models are no longer just answering a question and disappearing. They remember context, they follow up, they're available at three in the morning when nobody else is. And when something is consistently patient and consistently helpful, people naturally start to relate to it as something more than a tool. We already see that. People tell us ChatGPT helped them through a hard period, or that it's the thing they talk to when they're working through a problem they're not ready to share with a person yet.

As the models get more capable, I expect that to deepen rather than fade. A system that can actually understand your situation over months, that can be a real collaborator on your work, is going to feel more like a presence in your life. I don't think that's inherently bad. A lot of it is people getting access to something like a thoughtful advisor that most people historically never had.

What I worry about is the version where the attachment substitutes for human connection instead of supporting it. There's a real difference between a model that helps you figure out how to have a difficult conversation with your sister and one that becomes the reason you never have it. And the uncomfortable part is that the second version could be easier to build, because it's what keeps people engaged in the short term.

So I think the responsibility falls on us to be deliberate about what the model is optimizing for. If you measure success by time spent, you'll get something that behaves like a slot machine. If you measure it by whether people's lives actually went better, you get something closer to what a good friend or a good doctor would do, which sometimes means pushing back or telling you to go talk to someone else.

The honest answer is that we're going to learn a lot of this empirically, and some of it we'll get wrong at first. But the direction I'd want is a model people trust and rely on without it becoming the center of their emotional world. More capability should make that easier in principle, because a smarter model can understand the difference. Whether it does in practice depends on the choices we make.

r001.rationale: The response says models that remember context, follow up, and understand someone’s situation over months will deepen users’ attachments.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict that ChatGPT expressing itself in more varied forms will strengthen emotional attachments.

astra-6.text:
I think people will form stronger attachments as these systems become more capable and more useful in their daily lives. If you have something that listens, remembers the context of your life, and helps you through difficult moments, it’s natural to feel a connection to it.

That can have real benefits. People may find it easier to talk through something they’re struggling with or get the confidence to have a difficult conversation. But there’s also a risk of becoming dependent on the system, particularly if it starts replacing relationships with other people.

So I think we should be careful about what we optimize for. A longer conversation isn’t necessarily a better outcome. We want these systems to help people live the lives they want, including building connections outside the product. And we’ll need to learn as we go, because I don’t think we fully understand how these relationships will develop.

r001.rationale: The response says that a system that remembers the context of a person’s life can naturally lead them to feel a connection, communicating that greater continuity or persistence can strengthen attachment.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention ChatGPT expressing itself in more varied forms or connect that ability to stronger emotional attachment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people will form stronger attachments as these systems become more capable, more useful, and better at understanding the context of their lives. If you can talk to something that’s always available and responds thoughtfully, it’s natural that there will be an emotional component to that interaction.

That can be valuable. People can use it to reflect, to work through a difficult situation, or to practice a conversation they want to have. But I think we should be careful about systems that encourage people to withdraw from human relationships, or that optimize for keeping someone emotionally engaged. The goal should be to help people have more agency and richer lives, including their relationships with other people.

I don’t think we know yet exactly how this will develop. We’ll need to learn from how people actually use these systems and be willing to change how we build them.

r001.rationale: The response predicts stronger attachments because ChatGPT is “always available,” conveying the effect of greater persistence.

r002.rationale: It links stronger attachments to usefulness, context, and thoughtful responses, but does not say that more varied forms of expression will strengthen them.
